articles.title: How to Cut Hosting Costs by Self-Hosting Your Apps on a VPS (2026)
articles.excerpt: Managed platforms are priced per app, per seat, per build minute or per gigabyte of bandwidth. That's fair when you have one big app. It adds up fast when you're a freelancer or a small team running t…
articles.body: Managed platforms are priced per app, per seat, per build minute or per gigabyte of bandwidth. That's fair when you have one big app. It adds up fast when you're a freelancer or a small team running ten small ones: client sites, internal tools, side projects, staging copies. A single Linux VPS can often host all of them. This guide explains how to work out whether self-hosting actually saves you money, how to consolidate apps safely, and where tools like ShipOwn reduce the time cost that usually eats the savings. We won't quote prices here because they change constantly and depend on your region and usage. Use your own invoices for the maths below. Step 1: Audit what you pay for today Make a simple table from your last three invoices: App Platform Monthly cost Traffic Needs always-on?
articles.author: Vishvajeet Shukla

articles.title: Custom Domain + Free SSL on a VPS: Nginx and Certbot Done Right (2026)
articles.excerpt: Your app is running on the server. curl localhost:3000 works. Now you want https://app.example.com with a padlock, and that last mile (DNS, Nginx, certificates, renewals) is where a surprising number…
articles.body: Your app is running on the server. curl localhost:3000 works. Now you want https://app.example.com with a padlock, and that last mile (DNS, Nginx, certificates, renewals) is where a surprising number of deploys go wrong. This guide covers custom domains and free HTTPS on a Linux VPS end to end, plus how ShipOwn automates it safely. How the pieces fit DNS maps app.example.com to your server's IP. Nginx listens on ports 80/443 and decides which app gets each request, based on the server_name . Certbot proves to Let's Encrypt that you control the domain and installs a certificate into Nginx. Renewal replaces the certificate before it expires.
articles.author: Vishvajeet Shukla

articles.title: The 500MB Trap: Why We Moved Video Compression from Cloud to Browser with WebCodecs
articles.excerpt: Let's be brutally honest: the era of "free" commercial cloud services processing your heavy multimedia files is rapidly ending, if it's not already gone. You've seen it. That all-too-familiar moment w…
articles.body: Let's be brutally honest: the era of "free" commercial cloud services processing your heavy multimedia files is rapidly ending, if it's not already gone. You've seen it. That all-too-familiar moment when you try to compress a 4K video, even a modest one, only to be greeted by a hard 500MB file size limit and a prompt demanding $19.99/month for a "Pro" plan. Suddenly, a simple task that feels like it should happen locally on your powerful machine becomes a costly, slow, and privacy-questionable round trip to some vendor's overloaded cloud infrastructure. This isn't just an annoyance; it's a fundamental architectural challenge for any application dealing with user-generated media. We faced this exact predicament at SolveMyMedia.

articles.title: Dead miles are eating your gig pay — here's how to count them
articles.excerpt: You get paid for the miles with a passenger or an order in the car. You do not get paid for the miles to the pickup, between jobs, repositioning to a busier area, or driving home empty. Those unpaid m…
articles.body: You get paid for the miles with a passenger or an order in the car. You do not get paid for the miles to the pickup, between jobs, repositioning to a busier area, or driving home empty. Those unpaid miles are called dead miles, and they still cost you fuel and wear on your vehicle. That is why two shifts with the same pay can leave you with very different profit. The shift with more dead miles cost you more to do. What counts as a dead mile? Driving to your first pickup Driving between drop-off and the next pickup Moving to a busier area while waiting for work Driving home empty at the end of a shift Paid miles come from the gig app. Dead miles are everything else you drove for work.
articles.author: Abdullah Naseer

articles.body: While everyone has been arguing about whether there's an AI bubble, China quietly had one, and it has already popped. China's STAR50 index of AI and chip companies has fallen about 40% from its July high in under four months , erasing roughly $480 billion in market value, according to Reuters. The broader CSI300 is in bear-market territory. The Nasdaq, meanwhile, is only about 6% off its record. I'm a developer, not a fund manager. But this story is more relevant to people who build with AI than it looks, so here's my developer's-eye summary. The 30-second version The rally: Beijing pushed AI and chip self-sufficiency, and investors bet that "government-backed" meant "can't lose." The IPO frenzy: GPU maker MetaX closed its first trading day up 693% .

articles.title: How 'spacewalking' underwater made me feel like I was really in space
articles.excerpt: Analog Astronaut Commander and Aquanaut Michaela Musilova led underwater simulated “spacewalks” in low visibility to test astronaut safety and communication protocols during simulated space missions.
articles.body: I was breathing just fine through my life support systems, but I kept feeling an urge to double check that everything was ok with my "spacesuit" before heading out on this "spacewalk." I have worn many different types of spacesuits on Earth during my career, but for the first time in my life, I knew that I couldn’t just stop to breathe the air outside if there were an emergency. That's because I was underwater. On this excursion, I was leading a simulated space mission underwater called SEA STAR. My " spacesuit " was actually scuba diving gear, and the simulated spacewalks , or EVAs (Extra-Vehicular Activities), included outings where we explored underwater environments.

articles.excerpt: The four volunteers who lived and worked in a simulated NASA Mars mission for more than a year will exit their habitat on Saturday, Oct. 31, after 378 days of isolation in a facility at the agency’s J…
articles.body: Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA) Mission 2 crew members (from left) Ross Elder, Matthew Montgomery, Ellen Ellis, and James Spicer, pose for a photo on Oct. 8, 2025. Credit: NASA The four volunteers who lived and worked in a simulated NASA Mars mission for more than a year will exit their habitat on Saturday, Oct. 31, after 378 days of isolation in a facility at the agency’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. Health and performance data collected from the simulation can help NASA develop methods to counter human spaceflight risks for future Artemis and Moon Base missions. Beginning at 3 p.m. EDT, NASA will provide live coverage of the volunteers’ departure from the Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA, pronounced cha-pea’-ah) mission habitat.
